title: Slipped disc (herniated disc)
intro: A slipped disc occurs when some of the soft centre of a spinal disc pushes through its tougher outer layer and may press on a nearby nerve. It can cause back pain, and when a nerve is affected, pain, numbness or weakness in a leg or arm. Most people recover within weeks to months without surgery.

sections.heading: What happens
paragraphs: Between the vertebrae lie discs that act as cushions. With age or strain, the outer ring can weaken and the inner material bulge or leak. The lower back and the neck are most often affected. A bulge does not always cause symptoms, and scans often show disc changes in people without any pain.

sections.heading: Symptoms
paragraphs: A lumbar disc problem may cause sudden or gradual back pain with pain radiating down one leg, often below the knee, called sciatica, along with tingling, numbness or weakness. A neck disc can cause neck pain and symptoms in the shoulder, arm or hand. Coughing, sneezing or bending often worsens pain.

sections.heading: Warning signs
paragraphs: Seek emergency help for numbness around the genitals or buttocks, loss of bladder or bowel control, progressive leg weakness or severe, worsening symptoms in both legs. These can signal severe pressure on nerves needing urgent treatment.

sections.heading: Treatment without surgery
paragraphs: Most slipped discs improve by themselves, often within six weeks. Stay as active as pain allows and avoid bed rest. Painkillers, heat and gentle movement help, and physiotherapy with exercises supports recovery. Injections near the nerve can give short-term relief in selected cases. Scans are usually only needed when symptoms persist or warning signs occur.

sections.heading: Surgery
paragraphs: Surgery to remove the part of the disc pressing on the nerve is considered when severe pain or weakness persists despite several weeks of treatment or when nerve damage progresses. It relieves leg pain faster than waiting in many people but carries risks such as infection, nerve injury and recurrence, and long-term outcomes are similar to conservative care. Rehabilitation after surgery is important.

examples.title: Staying active
examples.text: Imagine you develop sciatica after lifting. You could keep walking short distances, avoid long periods of lying down, and ask about physiotherapy.

examples.title: Weighing surgery
examples.text: Suppose your leg pain has lasted three months. You might ask a spine specialist how likely surgery is to help, what the risks are and what recovery requires.
